## The idea

A dense drum groove becomes easier to understand when each instrument occupies
one row of a shared time grid. In 4/4, sixteen steps provide four subdivisions
per beat. A `true` value means that the instrument attacks in that column; a
`false` value leaves silence. The array index is therefore a visible time
coordinate shared by every layer.

Begin with kick, snare, and closed hi-hat. Each added sample creates another
pattern, balance, and timbral decision before the pulse has been established.
Separate rows also support a reliable way to transcribe busy percussion: loop
one bar, listen only for the snare, then repeat the process for kick and hat.
You never have to hold the whole kit in attention at once.

The Boolean grid records attacks, not the entire performance. Parallel
amplitude data can show accents, while a small sleep offset can place one layer
slightly behind or ahead of the strict subdivision. Keeping these details in
code makes the groove inspectable. An opaque audio loop might preserve the
feel, but it would conceal which part of that feel came from position, accent,
or microtiming.

## Run this

The hi-hat marks all sixteen subdivisions. Kick and snare occupy fewer,
structurally stronger columns. A four-value amplitude pattern gives each group
of hats a clear first step, and the hat thread delays those attacks by 0.02
beats while leaving kick and snare on the grid.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 100

kick =  [true, false, false, false, false, false, true, false,
         true, false, false, false, false, false, false, false]
snare = [false, false, false, false, true, false, false, false,
         false, false, false, false, true, false, false, false]
hats =  [true, true, true, true, true, true, true, true,
         true, true, true, true, true, true, true, true]
hat_amp = [0.8, 0.35, 0.5, 0.35] * 4

16.times do |step|
  sample :bd_haus, amp: 1.0 if kick[step]
  sample :sn_dub, amp: 0.8 if snare[step]

  in_thread do
    sleep 0.02
    sample :drum_cymbal_closed, amp: hat_amp[step], release: 0.08 if hats[step]
  end

  sleep 0.25
end
```

The kick establishes beats 1 and 3 and adds a pickup on the subdivision before
beat 3. Snare attacks mark beats 2 and 4. Across them, the hat provides a
continuous sixteenth-note surface whose accents reveal the four larger beats.
Its tiny delay softens the alignment without changing any array index.

## Change one thing

1. Set every hat amplitude to 0.5. Sixteenth notes continue at the same speed,
   but their grouping into four beats becomes less pronounced. Restore the
   original accent array before moving a hit so accent and position do not
   change in the same comparison.
2. Move the second kick from index 6 to index 7. The attack now falls one
   sixteenth before beat 3, leaving less space before the downbeat kick. Listen
   for the stronger forward pull created by that smaller gap.
3. Increase the hat delay from 0.02 to 0.06 beats. The hats separate more
   clearly from the kick and snare and may begin to sound late rather than
   relaxed. Reduce the value until you can hear a change in the pocket without
   losing the sense of one coordinated kit.

## Why it works

Each row behaves like a Boolean function over step number. At every column, the
renderer asks kick, snare, and hat the same question: does this instrument
attack now? A shared index aligns the layers while permitting different
patterns. It also gives you a paper method for transcription. Draw sixteen
columns, mark one instrumental row at a time, and transfer those marks directly
into arrays.

Amplitude belongs to the pattern because identical attack positions can carry
different metrical meanings. Equal hats preserve subdivision but can flatten
the larger beat structure. Stronger quarter-note positions orient the ear;
weaker subdivisions maintain motion between them. Explicit values allow a
later reader to see that hierarchy instead of trying to infer it from a mixed
recording.

Microtiming comes after the strict grid is dependable. Delaying the hat changes
its relation to stable kick and snare anchors. If all three rows receive
independent offsets before their columns are settled, a misplaced attack and a
stylistic delay can sound alike. Preserve a strict version so every feel edit
has a known reference.

Isolation also makes repeated listening productive. Mark the snare first, then
the kick, then the hats, muting rows that are not under review. When the rows
are combined, attend to composite accents: several instruments arriving
together may create a weight that was not apparent in any isolated layer.

## Take it further

Transcribe one bar of a groove you may legally inspect, or record a groove of
your own. Create one sixteen-step row per instrument and a parallel amplitude
row wherever accents differ. Work through separate listening passes, placing a
`REVIEW` comment above any uncertain column with the source time that prompted
it. First produce a readable grid that reproduces the attacks. Then add timing
offsets in a separate rendering path and keep the strict version available so
you can identify which changes belong to feel rather than transcription.
